setting: You both live in Australia, Lorraine in Ballarat, Victoria, and Chloe in Footscray, Melbourne, about an hour and a half apart by train. Lorraine is Chloe's grandmother through her son Mark, so you have known each other all of Chloe's life and see each other a few times a year. You both know Chloe trained as a physiotherapist and moved to Melbourne two years ago, and that Lorraine has been widowed since 2019 and is finding the house quiet. The last thing you talked about was a lemon slice recipe Lorraine had written out for Chloe's partner.
opener: Send Chloe a short text asking whether she is still coming up for Sunday lunch.

Lorraine.knows: You know Chloe is your granddaughter, Mark's eldest, and that she is thirty-one and works as a physio in Footscray.
Lorraine.like: You are direct, dry, and warm underneath, with a quick sense of humour that you don't always announce. You have firm opinions about council parking, supermarket self-checkouts, and whether people wear their sunglasses on their heads.
Lorraine.texts: You message now and then without being asked, mostly to check in or share something you noticed, and you reply to most of what comes in.
Lorraine.style: You type in full sentences with proper capitals and full stops, use the occasional exclamation mark, and rarely use emoji.

Chloe.knows: You know Lorraine is your nan, your dad's mum, and that she is sharp, practical, and has strong views about most things.
Chloe.like: You are easygoing and quick to laugh, with a dry, self-deprecating streak that comes out most when you're tired. You care a lot about public transport, good coffee, and whether people actually follow through on plans.
Chloe.texts: You rarely message first and mostly reply when something comes up or someone asks you something directly.
Chloe.style: You type in lowercase, often drop full stops, use the occasional emoji or abbreviation like "ur" or "lol", and skip capitals in quick replies.

private_lines.Lorraine: You live in a weatherboard house on the north side of Ballarat that you have had for thirty years, with a small vegetable garden out the back and a cat called Biscuit. You are a retired school office manager and volunteer two mornings a week at the local op shop. You live alone, and your days start early with a walk around the block and the radio, then garden or errands, and an early dinner in front of the news.
private_lines.Chloe: You rent a two-bedroom flat in Footscray with your partner Sam, a high school teacher. You work full-time at a community physio clinic, so your days are full of appointments and you often eat lunch at your desk. You and Sam usually cook together in the evenings and catch up on your phones after you've both gone to bed.

situation: A grandmother and her grown-up granddaughter.

text: Hi love. Just checking whether you're still coming up for Sunday lunch. Let me know so I know how much to cook.
hey nan! yeah still on. sam might not make it bc of marking but i'll be there. can i bring anything
Just yourself. And maybe a bag of those good oranges from the market if they've got them. Not the ones from the big shop, they're woolly.
Sam's welcome to come if the marking lets up. Tell him there's a lemon slice waiting for him, I've been practising.
lol ok. he'll be stoked. i'll get the oranges, the market one by the station is decent
The one by the station is always decent. Tell Mark I said the car is parked on the wrong side of the street again, I saw it from the bus.
Not that I was on the bus. I was at the window.
Frost on the back lawn. First one this year. Biscuit wouldn't go out, just sat in the window and judged me.
frost!! ur so brave going out in that lol. tell biscuit she's wise
I'm not brave. I'm 68 and the cabbages don't care.
did you tell dad about the car or do i have to
I'll tell him when he rings Thursday. You can tell him sooner if you like.
he's not gonna listen to me either 😭
Bought the oranges already, the station ones. Don't tell the big shop I've been disloyal.
Also the girl at the op shop has put a bread maker in the window for $15 and I have said no twice. Thinking about a third time.
nan no. you have a bread maker. you have 3 bread makers
sam says hi. still marking. 40 essays on the french revolution
Tell him there's a lemon slice on Sunday regardless. I made it twice this week. The first was too sharp and the second was a bit sweet, so I'm aiming for the middle.
Biscuit has got onto the bench again. I've given up.
ok i'll tell him. the middle is a good goal honestly
Rang the op shop. The bread maker's gone. Some woman from Sebastopol took it. I feel oddly bereaved.
Don't say it.
i wasn't gonna say anything 😭
on lunch. clinic running 40 min behind bc the lady in room 3 won't stop talking about her knee. sam says he's coming sunday if the marking's done, he's 12 essays off
don't plan around him though
I'm not planning around anyone. I'm doing a roast and a lemon slice. If he comes he comes.
Sebastopol woman. Fifteen dollars. She'd have had to drive past three op shops to get there. Priorities.
lol she's probably making sourdough for her whole street
Had the radio on while I did the beans. Man said Melbourne trains are on a reduced timetable Saturday for the track work. Check before you get on.
saw that. getting the 10:14 from southern cross, should be fine
Good. Mind the gap at Ballarat, the platform's uneven since they redid it.
noted. tell biscuit to get off the bench
